title: Graph Representation and Problem Modeling
summary: Clarify direction, weights, and states before choosing an adjacency list or matrix.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: A graph consists of vertices and edges. Vertices need not be cities: they may represent words, board positions, or search states. A directed edge permits movement only along its arrow, whereas an undirected edge allows travel in either direction. Before modeling the problem, specify the range of vertex labels, whether self-loops and parallel edges are allowed, and what to return for an empty graph. These conventions affect the correctness of subsequent algorithms.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: An adjacency list stores the outgoing edges of each vertex, so traversing a vertex examines only edges that actually exist. An adjacency matrix uses a two-dimensional table to record whether two vertices are connected. Edge lookup is convenient, but storage is quadratic. Adjacency lists usually suit sparse graphs; a matrix may be more intuitive when frequently querying relationships between vertex pairs or implementing dense-graph algorithms.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: An undirected edge must be stored in both directions in an adjacency list; a directed edge is stored once. A weighted graph can store each entry as a tuple containing the destination vertex and weight. One input edge is not the same thing as one stored adjacency entry. Although an undirected traversal examines every edge twice, its overall complexity remains linear.

For example, in a road problem, two roads are connected only when they share an endpoint. If their drawings cross without a junction, do not invent a new vertex. When edge weights represent travel time and directions represent one-way restrictions, both pieces of information must be retained. Also establish whether labels are consecutive: string names can first be mapped to integers before allocating arrays, avoiding confusion between application names and array positions.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: The template below builds directed or undirected graphs and validates endpoint ranges. Isolated vertices still receive empty lists, so they are not lost by inferring the vertex count from the edges. The template retains parallel edges and self-loops. If the problem requires a simple graph, deduplicate by destination; for parallel weighted edges, retain the minimum weight rather than arbitrarily overwriting it.

time: O(V+E), where V is the number of vertices and E is the number of input edges.
space: O(V+E), including the output adjacency list.

walkthrough: Vertex 2 has no edges but still requires an empty adjacency list.

pitfalls: Do not add an undirected edge in only one direction.
Do not use 0 to represent both a missing edge and a zero-weight edge.

title: Depth-First Search: Explore Along a Branch
summary: DFS uses a stack to hold pending states and suits connectivity and structural analysis.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: Depth-first search starts at a vertex, follows one branch deeper, and then returns to branches that remain unprocessed. It can use either the recursive call stack or an explicit stack. Here we consider a directed graph already represented by an adjacency list. Only vertices reachable from the starting vertex are visited, and their order depends on the ordering of adjacency lists.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Maintain a seen set of discovered vertices. Mark each new vertex immediately upon discovery, then push it onto the stack. This invariant ensures that every vertex enters the stack at most once, even with cycles, self-loops, or multiple predecessors. The stack represents work still to be processed; membership in seen does not imply that all of a vertex's outgoing edges have been processed.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: When vertex u is popped, inspect all its outgoing edges and push any undiscovered neighbors. Every reachable vertex has a path from the start. Considering this path one edge at a time, processing each predecessor necessarily discovers the next vertex, so no reachable vertex is missed. Unreachable vertices have no valid chain of exploration and therefore never enter the result.

Detecting a cycle in a directed graph requires distinguishing vertices on the current path from those whose processing has finished. A discovered neighbor does not necessarily indicate a cycle: two branches may simply reach the same vertex. Ordinary DFS seen flags answer only whether a vertex has been discovered. Three-color states can identify a back edge to a current ancestor.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: An explicit stack avoids Python's recursion-depth limit on long chains. The template scans neighbors in reverse so earlier neighbors are popped first, but marking them early can make the complete visitation order differ from recursive DFS. If entry and exit events are needed, as in topological analysis, use stack frames that record the current iterator position.

time: O(V+E); when scanning only the reachable subgraph, use its corresponding vertex and edge counts.
space: O(V) for the visited set, result, and stack.

walkthrough: 0 discovers 1, 1 discovers 2, and the neighbor 0 of 2 is already marked, ending the search.

pitfalls: Marking only when popping can cause repeated stack entries.
An ordinary seen set cannot distinguish back edges from completed branches in a directed graph.

title: Breadth-First Search: Levels Count Edges
summary: In an unweighted graph, first discovery gives the minimum number of edges to a vertex.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: Breadth-first search first processes vertices one edge from the start, then those two edges away, expanding outward level by level. Every edge here has unit cost, and the graph may be directed. The goal is to return the minimum edge-count distance to every vertex, using -1 for unreachable vertices. The starting distance is zero, not one.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: The queue stores vertices in nondecreasing distance order. Processing a vertex at distance d discovers only neighbors at distance d+1, so appending new states to the back preserves level order. Once a vertex is discovered, its distance never needs updating. If a shorter path existed, its predecessor would have left the queue earlier, contradicting the first discovery.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Start by enqueuing the source. After removing u, inspect v on every outgoing edge. If v is undiscovered, set dist[v]=dist[u]+1 and enqueue it. This step both marks v and establishes its shortest distance. Vertices still labeled -1 after the search have no path from the source; their sentinel values must not participate in distance comparisons.

When several starting vertices all have initial cost zero, set all their distances to zero and enqueue them together. This is multi-source BFS. It is equivalent to adding a virtual source at level zero and computes the distance to the nearest source, rather than the sum of distances to all sources. Nearest-exit and propagation-time problems on grids often use this variation.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: Use collections.deque and popleft in Python to remove the front item in constant time. A regular list's pop(0) moves many elements. The function below validates the source. To reconstruct a route, additionally record parent[v]=u upon first discovery, then trace backward from the destination to the source.

time: O(V+E).
space: O(V).

walkthrough: 1 and 2 are on the same level.
The distance to 3 is already shortest when it is first discovered.
4 retains the unreachable marker.

pitfalls: Ordinary BFS cannot be used directly when edge weights differ.
Mark upon discovery, rather than waiting until dequeueing.

title: 797. All Paths From Source to Target
summary: Backtrack through a DAG while maintaining the current path; copy it whenever the target is reached.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: Given a directed acyclic graph with vertices numbered 0 through n-1, enumerate all paths from 0 to n-1. A path is identified by its vertex sequence, and the problem usually guarantees no duplicate outgoing edges. Acyclicity matters: it guarantees that each branch terminates and removes the need for a separate visited set to prevent cycles within the current path.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Maintain path as the complete route from the source to the current vertex. Append a neighbor before entering it and pop it after returning, restoring the state from before that branch. A global visited set must not prevent repeated arrivals here: distinct prefixes can merge at an intermediate vertex, and the paths after the merge must count separately for each prefix.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Upon reaching the target, copy path into the result and return immediately. The copy is essential; otherwise the answers reference the same mutable list, whose contents disappear as backtracking finishes. Enumerating every outgoing edge at each vertex enumerates all possible next steps, so no valid path is omitted. Every decision sequence is generated once.

Even when the target is unreachable, backtracking may enumerate many prefixes that ultimately fail. First marking vertices that can reach the target in the reverse graph allows the search to skip other branches. This pruning removes no answer, since every suffix of a valid path must reach the target. However, preprocessing cannot eliminate the exponential growth of the output itself.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: The recursive code illustrates backtracking and suits the small DAGs in this problem. An empty graph returns no paths; a one-vertex graph returns the path containing only the source. Recursion depth is at most V. For long DAGs in production, use an explicit backtracking stack. The number of outputs can be exponential, so this is not an ordinary O(V+E) traversal.

time: O(V·2^V) is a loose upper bound for a simple DAG; actual work depends on the explored prefixes and total output length.
space: O(V) working space, plus output space equal to the total length of all answers.

walkthrough: Save a copy after following 0→1→3.
Backtrack to 0, then follow 0→2→3.

pitfalls: A global visited set loses paths with different prefixes that later merge.
Cyclic input violates the algorithm's precondition.

title: 200. Number of Islands: DFS
summary: Each search from an unvisited land cell discovers a new connected component.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: In the grid, the string '1' denotes land and '0' denotes water. Land cells connect only up, down, left, or right. The goal is to count separate land regions, rather than land cells. Diagonal contact does not merge islands. The implementation below preserves the original grid and records discoveries in a visited set, allowing the input to be reused after the call.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Scan the grid. Whenever an unvisited land cell is found, increment the island count and use DFS to mark all land connected to it. The invariant is that once this search finishes, every cell of this island has been marked and no other island has been marked accidentally, since exploration crosses only valid land-adjacency edges.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Each island has a first cell encountered in scan order. Earlier searches cannot have covered that cell, so it triggers exactly one increment. Later cells of the same island are already marked and trigger none. This one-to-one correspondence proves that the answer counts islands, rather than DFS branches, and does not depend on the ordering of search directions.

If modifying the grid is allowed, change discovered land to water and use the input itself as the visited marker. This removes seen, but an explicit stack can still require linear space in the worst case; total extra space does not become constant. Tell callers that the grid has changed, or a repeated call will unexpectedly report zero islands.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: The explicit stack implements DFS. Mark neighbors immediately when discovered to prevent multiple cells from pushing the same neighbor. Check bounds before reading grid[nr][nc]. An empty grid returns zero, and the implementation assumes a rectangular grid. Compare explicitly against '1' in a character grid: string truthiness does not identify water.

time: O(RC), where R and C are the numbers of rows and columns.
space: O(RC) for visited records and the stack.

walkthrough: The two land cells touch only diagonally, so each starts its own DFS.

pitfalls: The string '0' is truthy.
Do not count diagonal directions as connections.

title: 200. Number of Islands: BFS
summary: Expand an entire island with a queue, counting only the first cell of each new island during the scan.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: An island still consists of four-directionally connected '1' cells, but breadth-first search now expands the region. Counting islands does not require shortest paths: both BFS and DFS correctly traverse connected components. Choosing a queue primarily changes exploration order. The connection structure determines the number of islands, regardless of whether exploration proceeds by levels or depth.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: The outer scan searches for undiscovered land. Mark the cell, enqueue it, and increment the answer. The queue holds cells of this island that still need expansion, while seen contains all discovered cells. On removing a cell, inspect its four neighbors, mark newly found land, and enqueue it. Every cell is removed and expanded only once.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: When the queue empties, every cell reachable through this island's land has been discovered. If a cell of the same island remained undiscovered, consider the first undiscovered cell on a path from the starting cell to it. Its predecessor must already have been dequeued and should have discovered it, a contradiction. Consequently, later cells on this island are not counted again, while the next island correctly triggers another count.

A BFS level contains land at the same edge-count distance from the starting cell, but counting happens only when the outer scan starts a search, not at the beginning of every level. A long, narrow island may span many levels and still be one island. A broad island may create a large queue and still increment the answer only once. Level count, queue length, and island count are three different concepts.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: The code uses deque for constant-time removal. The visited set could be replaced by a Boolean matrix. If input modification is allowed, change discovered '1' cells to '0', doing so upon enqueueing. This version preserves the input and handles empty grids. A very wide island can produce a large queue, so space cannot simply be stated as a grid side length.

time: O(RC).
space: O(RC).

walkthrough: The first two land cells are marked in the same queue-based search.
The last land cell starts a separate BFS.

pitfalls: A regular list's pop(0) introduces element-shifting costs.
Marking only after dequeueing causes repeated enqueues.

title: 695. Max Area of Island
summary: Count the cells in each connected component and take the largest count.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: In an integer grid, 1 denotes land and 0 denotes water. Islands are defined by four-directional connectivity. Area is the number of cells on one island, rather than its perimeter or bounding-rectangle area. Return the cell count of the largest island, or zero if there is no land. A general component search below collects all coordinates of each island.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: The components function assigns each land cell to exactly one group. DFS adds each popped cell to the current component and marks neighbors when pushing them, preventing repeated area contributions. The length of a group is the island's area. Take the maximum length across all groups; island location and discovery order do not affect the result.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Why not count consecutive 1s in each row? An island can turn across rows and have a highly irregular shape; a four-directional search captures its full connectivity. Conversely, a bounding rectangle may contain water or other islands, so row and column spans cannot estimate the area. Counting cells during the search exactly matches the definition, and correctness follows directly from the component partition.

A snake-shaped island can span many rows and columns yet have a small area, whereas a solid block nearly fills its bounding rectangle. Computing area requires neither DFS parents nor route reconstruction: only component membership matters. Each discovered cell belongs to a unique group and must be skipped on later encounters, or the area will be counted repeatedly.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: The template preserves the original grid and stores every coordinate group for clarity and reuse. If only the maximum area is needed, maintain an integer counter inside DFS and update the maximum afterward, avoiding storage of all groups. The visited records still require linear space. Using max with default=0 explicitly handles all-water and empty grids.

time: O(RC); each land cell checks four neighbors.
space: O(RC) for visited records, the stack, and component coordinates.

walkthrough: The three upper-left cells connect; the other two land cells form separate islands.
The areas are 3, 1, and 1, so the maximum is 3.

pitfalls: Land values are integers, not strings.
Count the whole component, rather than a single DFS branch.

title: 1020. Number of Enclaves
summary: Land components touching the boundary can escape; sum the areas of the remaining components.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: This problem counts land cells that cannot reach the outside of the grid by walking on land. Leaving the grid requires crossing a boundary land cell. Therefore, if a component contains any boundary cell, its entire land area can escape. The answer is the total area of land enclosed inside, rather than the number of interior islands or the number of cells not directly adjacent to the boundary.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: First partition land into four-directionally connected components. Check whether each component contains a cell in row 0 or R-1, or column 0 or C-1. If it does, exclude the whole group; otherwise add len(group). All cells of a component can reach each other, so the ability to escape is a property of the entire component.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: For a component touching the boundary, every cell can first follow a land path to the boundary and then step out of the grid. For a component not touching the boundary, any route out must first reach a boundary cell, but the component contains no such land cell. Hence no escape path exists. Together, these arguments prove the filtering condition both necessary and sufficient.

Consider interior land connected to the boundary by a narrow corridor. Most cells may be far from the boundary, but all can still escape. Removing boundary cells without continuing the search would incorrectly count the land behind the corridor as enclaves. Evaluate whole connected components, or propagate from the boundary until no further cells can be reached, rather than inspecting just the perimeter cells.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: The code reuses components and preserves the input. An alternative performs a multi-source search from boundary land, marks all escapable cells, and then counts remaining land. It avoids retaining component coordinates and has the same time bound. With only one row or column, all land lies on the boundary, so the result is naturally zero.

time: O(RC).
space: O(RC).

walkthrough: The three land cells are connected.
Their component has no boundary cells, so all three contribute to the enclave area.

pitfalls: Interior cells connected to the boundary must also be excluded.
Return the total area, rather than the number of enclosed components.

title: 130. Surrounded Regions
summary: Preserve O cells connected to the boundary; flip the remaining O cells to X.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: On the character board, O cells form four-directionally connected regions and X cells block movement. Flip only regions fully surrounded by X that cannot reach the board boundary through O cells. The output is the complete board. This function returns a new two-dimensional list and preserves the caller's input. If an online judge requires in-place modification, assign the result back to board row by row.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Directly checking whether each interior O is surrounded repeatedly explores long paths. Instead, reverse the perspective: search from every boundary O and mark all O cells connected to the boundary as safe. Cells in this set must remain unchanged, and all remaining O cells belong to enclosed regions. A final full-board scan constructs the result.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: A boundary O is plainly not surrounded; any cell with an O-only path to it is likewise connected to the outside. The search travels only through O, so it cannot incorrectly add a cell across an X barrier to safe. Every O connected to the boundary has such a path and is eventually visited. Thus the preserved set is exactly the set of all cells that must not flip.

Do not immediately change every interior O to X before the safe search finishes: an unexamined interior cell may connect to the boundary through a distant corridor. Changing it early artificially blocks that corridor, making subsequent searches operate on a different graph. Complete the preserved set first, then transform characters together, separating classification from result construction.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: Use an explicit stack for multi-source DFS and have seed deduplicate cells before pushing them. The four board edges overlap at corners, and a single row or column may also be scanned repeatedly; deduplication handles these cases uniformly. Determine each output character using the original cell and safe. An empty board returns an empty list. Checking only whether the cell itself is on the boundary is insufficient, because its region may connect by a winding path.

time: O(RC).
space: O(RC), including the new output board.

walkthrough: The O on the bottom boundary is marked safe.
The three central O cells cannot reach the boundary and are all flipped.

pitfalls: Only four-directional adjacency counts.
This function returns a new board, so callers must use the return value.

tests.expression: [''.join(row) for row in capture([list(s) for s in ['XXXX','XOOX','XXOX','XOXX']])]

title: 417. Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
summary: Search inward from each coast toward higher or equal cells, then intersect the two reachable sets.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: Water can flow from a cell to a four-directional neighbor when the destination is no higher than the current cell. The top and left boundaries touch the Pacific, while the bottom and right boundaries touch the Atlantic. Find every coordinate from which water can reach both oceans. Simulating outward flow separately from every cell repeats work, so reverse the edges and search inward from the coasts.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: The original graph has an edge u→v exactly when height[v]≤height[u]. In the reversed graph, movement from v to u requires height[u]≥height[v], so reverse search expands only to higher or equal neighbors. The Pacific reachable set represents cells that can flow into the Pacific in the original graph; the Atlantic set has the corresponding meaning.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Start separate searches from all cells along each ocean's coastline. Reversing an original path that flows to a coast produces a reverse-graph path from that coast to the cell. Existence is equivalent in both directions. The intersection of the visited sets therefore contains exactly the cells with paths to both oceans. Those two water-flow paths need not be the same path.

In a one-row or one-column grid, every cell lies on a boundary of each ocean, so all cells qualify even when heights vary greatly. More generally, water can choose different directions to reach different oceans. A single drop need not follow one route that reaches one ocean and then the other: the requirement is the intersection of two path-existence conditions.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: The template uses iterative DFS. Convert multi-source coordinates to a set first to remove duplicate corners. Scan the grid in row-column order to produce coordinates belonging to both sets, so sorting is unnecessary and time remains O(RC). The height matrix is preserved. Each search must have its own seen set; sharing markers confuses the two distinct reachability relations.

time: O(RC); results are produced in grid order without sorting.
space: O(RC).

walkthrough: The upper-left cell can flow only to the Pacific.
Each of the other three cells has descending paths to both oceans.

pitfalls: Reverse search uses ≥, rather than the original flow condition ≤.
Equal-height cells allow flow in both directions.

title: 827. Making A Large Island
summary: Label islands and record their areas, then merge distinct neighboring islands for each 0.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: Change at most one water cell 0 into land 1 to maximize the final island area. A flip connects only islands adjacent to the cell in the four cardinal directions; it cannot directly connect distant islands. The implementation supports rectangular grids, with the original square grid as a special case. All-land input needs no flip; nonempty all-water input can create an island of area one.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: First use DFS to assign each island a unique label and record size[id]. Store the island label for every land cell. Then inspect each water cell and collect its four neighboring land labels in a set. The area after flipping is one plus the sum of the areas of these distinct islands. Deduplication is essential: the same island may touch a water cell from two or more directions.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Existing island areas supply a lower bound without flipping. After flipping a particular 0, the original land connected to it can belong only to its neighboring islands, and each neighboring island is itself fully connected. Thus the new island consists of exactly this cell and those islands. Enumerating every 0 and comparing its candidate area with the lower bound covers all allowed decisions.

A water cell enclosed by a ring of land may touch the same island on all four sides. If that island has area eight, flipping produces area nine, not thirty-three. Deduplicate by island label only: different islands of equal area must both be included, so deduplicating area values is incorrect. Precomputed labels make these situations easy to distinguish.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: The code obtains coordinate groups through components and writes them into labels. Labels start at one, reserving zero for water. The sizes dictionary prevents accidentally including water as an island contribution. Computing a candidate requires neither modifying the grid nor running DFS again for every 0, reducing repeated quadratic searches to one preprocessing pass and one scan.

time: O(RC); each set contains at most four labels.
space: O(RC).

walkthrough: Either water cell borders two distinct islands of area one.
Flipping it gives area 1+1+1=3.

pitfalls: Add each neighboring island's area only once.
For all-land input, initializing the result to zero and inspecting only water cells fails.

title: 463. Island Perimeter
summary: Start each land cell with four edges, then subtract edges shared with other land cells.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: The perimeter consists of unit edges where land touches water or the outside of the grid. Diagonal contact removes no edges. The original problem usually assumes one island with no lakes. This implementation more generally returns the total length of all land boundaries. If lakes exist, their shores are included, which differs from counting only the outer outline.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Each land cell initially contributes four edges. A shared edge between adjacent land cells is counted once by each cell but is not part of the boundary, so subtract two for each adjacent pair. Checking only the upper and left neighbors processes every pair exactly once and avoids repeatedly subtracting the same shared edge.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Add all four edges of every cell independently, then remove internal shared edges one by one. What remains is exactly the set of boundary edges. Checking above and left covers all horizontal and vertical adjacency pairs: the right cell handles a horizontal pair, and the lower cell handles a vertical pair. An outside edge or water-facing edge lacks two land endpoints and is never subtracted.

Alternatively, inspect four directions from each land cell and add one whenever the neighbor is out of bounds or water. This version avoids subtraction. Both approaches follow the local definition of a boundary and produce the same result. Checking only upper and left neighbors has a smaller constant factor; checking all four directions is more direct when outputting specific boundary positions. With no land, the contribution is naturally zero.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: The algorithm needs only a grid scan, without DFS or visited records, because the task concerns local adjacency contributions rather than component membership. In Python, check that r or c is nonzero before accessing the previous row or column to avoid negative-index wraparound. An empty grid returns zero. Rows are assumed to have equal lengths.

time: O(RC).
space: O(1), excluding the input.

walkthrough: Three cells initially contribute 12.
Subtract 2 for each of two shared edges to obtain 8.

pitfalls: Checking all four directions while subtracting two each time double-subtracts shared edges.
With lakes, the result includes lake shores.

title: 127. Word Ladder
summary: Treat one valid letter replacement as an unweighted edge and use BFS to find the shortest sequence length.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: Each step changes exactly one character, and the new word must belong to the dictionary. All words have the same length and contain only lowercase English letters. Return the length of the shortest word sequence from begin to end, including both endpoints, or zero if no transformation exists. The starting word need not belong to the dictionary; the ending word must belong when it differs from the start.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: There is no need to explicitly construct edges between every pair of words. When processing a word, try all twenty-six letters at each position to generate every one-step candidate, then check membership in the unvisited dictionary set. All valid transformations have equal cost, so BFS first discovers the target using the fewest transformation edges. Adding the starting word gives the requested sequence length.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: The queue stores pairs of a word and its current sequence length. Immediately remove discovered candidates from remaining so they cannot be enqueued again. This acts as a visited marker and prevents cycles caused by reversing replacements. Level order processes shorter sequences first, so once a word has been discovered, longer prefixes reaching it need not be retained.

The dictionary may contain duplicate words; converting it to a set leaves one state per distinct word. Returning all shortest ladders requires a different treatment: removing a state and discarding other predecessors from the same level loses answers. Record all shortest predecessors on that level and backtrack after distances are established. For the shortest length alone, one visit retains enough information.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: The template constructs candidate strings by slicing and concatenation. Each length-L candidate costs O(L) to construct, so complexity cannot be stated as merely O(NL). Equal endpoints return one, an explicit boundary convention in this version. Dictionary entries of other lengths are filtered out to keep implicit adjacency consistent with the input assumptions.

time: O(N·26·L²), where N is the number of distinct dictionary words and L is word length, including string construction and hashing.
space: O(NL) for strings in the dictionary set and queue.

walkthrough: hit→hot→dot→dog→cog requires four replacements.
The sequence contains five words, so return five.

pitfalls: Return the number of words, rather than replacements.
Remove candidates upon enqueueing to avoid repeated expansion.

title: Directed Graphs: Can the Source Reach Every Vertex?
summary: Search only outgoing edges; the source covers the graph exactly when the visited count equals the vertex count.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: Given a directed graph and a designated source, determine whether paths following arrow directions reach every vertex from that source. This is stronger than undirected connectivity but weaker than strong connectivity: other vertices need not be able to return to the source. Vertices are numbered 0 through n-1. Here an empty graph returns true without inspecting its meaningless source argument.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Run DFS from the source, expanding visited only along outgoing edges. While processing u, if u→v exists and v is unvisited, mark v and push it. Every discovered vertex has a source-to-vertex path made of search edges, so an edge facing the opposite direction is never mistaken for a valid route.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: After the search, visited is exactly the set reachable from the source. Every inserted vertex is reachable, and conversely, vertices on each reachable path are discovered in succession. Therefore, its size equals n exactly when the requested condition holds. To output unreachable vertices, take the complement of visited within all vertex labels.

For example, with edges 0→1 and 2→1, ignoring direction puts all three vertices in one component, but 0 cannot reach 2. An undirected connectivity test would incorrectly return true. If every vertex must reach a designated destination, reverse all edges and run the same search from that destination; the path-existence conditions correspond one to one.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: The template validates edge endpoints and, for nonempty graphs, the source range, preventing subtle Python negative-index errors. Union-find is unsuitable because it represents symmetric connectivity, not arrow-directed reachability. Finding some source that covers the entire graph requires additional candidate selection; this fixed-source function alone does not solve that different problem.

time: O(V+E).
space: O(V+E), including the adjacency list.

walkthrough: Following the arrows discovers 1 and then 2.
Starting from 2 instead would not allow a return in the reverse direction.

pitfalls: Do not store directed edges as bidirectional edges.
A source reaching every vertex does not imply strong connectivity.

title: Union-Find: Maintain Connected Components
summary: Path compression and union by size make dynamic connectivity queries nearly constant time.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: Union-find maintains a collection of disjoint sets. It supports find, which returns the representative of the set containing an element, and union, which merges two sets. It suits connectivity queries as undirected edges are added and is also used by Kruskal to detect cycles. The implementation initializes n independent elements, each in its own set.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: The parent pointers form a representative forest, whose roots satisfy parent[root]=root. find follows these pointers to the root. Two elements belong to the same set exactly when their roots match. A size entry represents the set size only at a root. Before merging, find both roots and attach the smaller tree's root to the larger tree's root, preventing continued growth into a chain.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Path compression shortens parent chains during queries without changing any element's set membership. Union by size also prevents tree heights from deteriorating unchecked before compression. If union finds equal roots, it returns False to indicate that the set structure did not change. Otherwise it returns True and updates the new root's size, supporting spanning-tree construction or component counting.

The label of a representative has no application-specific meaning. Union by size may attach a smaller-numbered vertex beneath a larger-numbered one. Queries should compare find results rather than require a particular member to be the representative. To track each component's minimum label, maintain an additional root statistic and merge it after every successful union.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: The code uses path halving: inside the loop, each element is redirected to its grandparent, avoiding recursion. Callers must ensure valid element labels; negative Python indices do not automatically raise errors. Union-find retains no actual graph paths and cannot directly handle edge deletions. Choose another structure or an offline method when routes or deletions are required.

time: O((n+m)α(n)) total amortized time for m operations, where α is the inverse Ackermann function.
space: O(n).

example.output: 0 and 2 belong to the same set
walkthrough: Initially there are four roots.
After two successful unions, 0, 1, and 2 share a representative; 3 remains separate.

pitfalls: A size entry at a nonroot is not a reliable current set size.
Union-find directly represents only symmetric connectivity equivalence relations.

title: 1971. Find if Path Exists in Graph
summary: An undirected path exists exactly when the two vertices belong to the same union-find set.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: Given an undirected graph and source and destination vertices, determine whether a path connects them. A path may contain any number of edges. If both endpoints are equal, a zero-edge path already exists. Isolated vertices are allowed, so initialize all n vertices rather than only labels appearing in the edge list.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Apply union to the two endpoints of every undirected edge. Each successful merge joins the components connected by the new edge; endpoints already in the same component cause no structural change. After all edges are processed, equal roots mean the vertices belong to the same undirected connected component, which is equivalent to the existence of a graph path.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Initially, each vertex connects only to itself, matching a graph with no edges. When edge u-v is added, newly created paths can connect only the previous component of u with the previous component of v; other components are unaffected. union performs exactly this set merge. Induction over edges shows that the union-find partition matches the actual connected components.

Union-find discards edge order and route details. Parent chains returned through find need not correspond to original graph edges, so the parent array is not a route from source to destination. To output a path, use BFS or DFS and record predecessors from the original graph. Union-find's advantage is most apparent with many reachability queries.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: DFS or BFS also solves a single query. Union-find preprocessing is more suitable when the same graph receives many vertex-pair queries. The template reuses union by size and path halving. It relies on the problem's guarantee of valid labels; for untrusted external input, first validate n, edge endpoints, and both queried vertices.

time: O((V+E)α(V)); a single root comparison takes amortized O(α(V)).
space: O(V), without constructing an additional adjacency list.

walkthrough: 0, 1, and 2 are merged.
3 remains an independent component.

pitfalls: This approach does not directly answer directed path queries.
The answer is true when source equals destination.

title: 684. Redundant Connection
summary: Insert edges in order; the first edge joining vertices already in the same component closes the cycle.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: The input is an undirected tree with one additional edge and vertex labels starting at one. Remove one edge to restore a tree. If several answers work, return the one occurring latest in the input. A tree has no cycles; adding one edge creates exactly one cycle, and any edge on it can be removed. Scanning in input order naturally enforces the latest-edge requirement.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Pass edges to union-find in input order. A successful union connects previously separate components and creates no cycle. A failed union means a path already connected the endpoints, so the new edge and that path form a cycle. Under this problem's assumptions, there is exactly one failed union: the last input edge belonging to the unique cycle.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Before the last cycle edge is scanned, all other cycle edges have already been inserted, so its endpoints are connected and its union must fail. Earlier in the scan, at least one cycle edge is still missing, so the unique cycle cannot be closed and no earlier failure occurs. Thus the first failure both detects the cycle and gives the latest valid answer in input order.

For example, if the cycle consists of 1-2, 2-3, and 3-1, other tree branches merely extend the forest during the scan and do not affect cycle detection. The redundant edge need not be the final input edge: it must be the last edge of the cycle. If the final input edge is a branch to a new leaf, its union succeeds and it must not be mistaken for the redundant edge.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: Because labels start at one, allocate a DSU one larger than the maximum label and leave index zero unused. Empty edge input returns an empty list, while nonempty input is interpreted under the tree-plus-one-edge assumption. A general graph may have several cycles. Its first failed union only identifies one cycle-closing edge and does not establish that removing it restores a tree spanning the graph.

time: O(Eα(V)), where V is determined by the maximum label.
space: O(V).

walkthrough: The first two edges connect all three vertices.
The last edge joins already connected endpoints and closes the unique cycle.

pitfalls: The input must be a tree plus one edge.
Labels starting at one require more than just V zero-based slots.

title: 685. Redundant Connection II
summary: Find a vertex with two parents, then test for a cycle after skipping a candidate edge.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: The input is a rooted directed tree with one additional directed edge, with vertices labeled one through n. A valid result requires the root to have indegree zero, every other vertex to have indegree one, and every vertex to be reachable from the root. The extra edge may create a directed cycle, give a vertex two parents, or do both. Undirected cycle detection alone does not handle all cases.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: First scan incoming edges. If a vertex v receives a second parent edge, record the earlier edge as first and the later edge as second. Temporarily skip second and apply union-find to the remaining edges. Every vertex now has indegree at most one, and the promised structure makes an undirected cycle check sufficient to identify the unique cycle that needs attention.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: If no vertex has two parents, the only problem is a cycle, so return the edge whose union fails. If there are two parents and skipping second removes all cycles, deleting second restores the tree and satisfies the preference for the later edge. If a cycle remains, first lies on that cycle and second does not break it; deleting first is required to eliminate both the two-parent conflict and the cycle.

For example, with edges 2→1, 3→1, 4→2, and 1→4, vertex 1 has two parents. Skipping 3→1 still leaves the cycle 2→1→4→2, so the earlier edge 2→1 must be removed. This shows that preferring the later edge applies only when its removal actually restores a rooted tree; always selecting the second parent edge without checking is incorrect.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: Record edge indices, rather than endpoints alone, to distinguish input order explicitly. parent_edge records incoming edges, whereas DSU.parent represents the set forest; their meanings differ. The code relies on the original vertex range and tree-plus-one-edge guarantee. A general directed graph cannot necessarily become a rooted tree by removing one edge through this procedure, so the conclusion cannot be generalized unconditionally.

time: O(Vα(V)); E=V for a tree plus one edge.
space: O(V).

walkthrough: Vertex 3 has two incoming edges.
Skipping the later edge 2→3 leaves no cycle, so remove it.

pitfalls: Handle the two-parent conflict first; finding a cycle-closing edge alone is insufficient.
The union-find cycle check relies on the tree-plus-one-edge structure.

title: Prim: Grow a Minimum Spanning Tree
summary: Choose the lightest edge connecting the selected set to an outside vertex at each step.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: A minimum spanning tree selects V-1 edges in a connected, undirected, weighted graph to connect all vertices with minimum total weight. It minimizes the cost of connecting the entire graph, unlike shortest paths from a source to each vertex. Weights may be negative, and parallel edges are allowed. This version returns the total weight, raises ValueError for a disconnected graph, and defines an empty graph's weight as zero.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Start from any vertex and maintain a selected set S. The heap contains candidate edges from S to outside vertices. Repeatedly pop the lightest edge whose endpoint is not yet selected, add that endpoint to S, and push all its outgoing edges. Skip old candidates pointing to selected vertices, ensuring that each successful selection introduces exactly one new vertex.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: The lightest edge crossing the cut between S and its complement is safe. If an optimal tree omits it, adding it forms a cycle. That cycle contains another crossing edge whose weight is no smaller. Replacing that edge yields another spanning tree of no greater weight. Thus every step remains compatible with some optimal tree, and including all vertices produces a minimum spanning tree.

The selected set needs only one initial entry. Afterward, every valid candidate comes from an outgoing edge of a selected vertex. The heap may contain two edges to the same outside vertex: the lighter one enters the tree first, and the heavier one is later discarded because its endpoint is already selected. This is lazy processing of boundary candidates. It does not sum source distances and need not calculate distances along the tree from the starting vertex.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: The template uses adjacency lists and heapq, storing weight-vertex pairs. The starting vertex is inserted as a virtual entry with weight zero. Comparing labels to break equal-weight ties does not change the total weight. The heap can hold O(E) entries, so its sorting factor must account for parallel edges with log E rather than assuming log V. If fewer than V vertices are selected, report disconnection.

time: O(V+E log(E+1)), allowing parallel edges.
space: O(V+E) for the adjacency list and heap.

walkthrough: From 0, select the weight-1 edge to connect 2.
The lightest crossing edge is 2→1 with weight 2, giving a total of 3.

pitfalls: Minimum spanning trees allow negative weights; Dijkstra's nonnegative-weight restriction does not apply.
For disconnected input, do not silently return the weight of a single component.

title: Kruskal: Merge Components in Edge-Weight Order
summary: Inspect edges from lightest to heaviest and accept only those joining different components.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: Kruskal constructs a minimum spanning tree of an undirected weighted graph by focusing on edges. Initially, every vertex is its own component. Sort edges by increasing weight and consider each for inclusion. Negative weights, equal weights, and parallel edges are allowed; self-loops are never needed. Define the empty graph's weight as zero and explicitly fail for disconnected input.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Union-find maintains the forest formed by accepted edges. If an edge's endpoints have different roots, accept it and merge the components. If their roots match, an existing path already connects them and adding the edge would create a cycle, so skip it. Each successful union reduces the component count by one, so a connected graph accepts exactly V-1 edges.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: When processing u-v whose endpoints remain in separate components, sorted order makes it a cheapest connection encountered for those current components. The cut property proves that accepting it is safe. Rejecting cycle-forming edges does not remove needed future connection possibilities from the forest. Repeatedly add safe edges until a single component remains, obtaining an acyclic connection of minimum weight.

Unlike Prim, which expands outward from one component, Kruskal may maintain many small trees simultaneously. The cheapest safe edge can lie between any two components. Both algorithms rely on the cut property rather than route lengths. To obtain a minimum spanning forest, remove the disconnected-graph error and retain all successfully merged edges, but make that change explicit in the interface name and return definition.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: The sorting key uses only the third element, the weight, to avoid accidentally sorting by vertex labels. The template tracks chosen and can stop once it reaches n-1. If scanning ends with fewer accepted edges, raise an exception. Sorting dominates the time, while nearly constant amortized DSU operations supply the filtering cost. To return the tree itself, also save edges on successful unions.

time: O(V+E log(E+1)+Eα(V)).
space: O(V+E) for the sorted copy and union-find.

walkthrough: After sorting, accept weight 1 and then weight 2.
Two edges now connect all three vertices, so stop.

pitfalls: Sort by weight.
Returning a forest's weight and returning a spanning tree's weight are different contracts.

title: Topological Sort: Dependencies Before Their Dependents
summary: Repeatedly remove indegree-zero vertices; processing fewer than all vertices reveals a directed cycle.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: A directed edge u→v means u must precede v. Topological sorting finds a permutation satisfying all such precedence constraints and is common in course prerequisites and task scheduling. Only directed acyclic graphs have topological orders. This is neither label sorting nor weight sorting, and one DAG often has several valid results.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Kahn's algorithm maintains each vertex's indegree in the graph that remains after removals. Indegree zero means no remaining predecessor constrains it, so it can enter the result. Removing a vertex also removes its outgoing edges, decrementing each destination's indegree. Enqueue a destination exactly when its indegree reaches zero.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Every output vertex has no predecessor that remains unprocessed, so no dependency is violated. If all vertices are processed, the result is a valid topological order. If the queue empties with vertices remaining, each has a remaining predecessor. Repeatedly following predecessors in a finite graph must revisit a vertex, forming a directed cycle; report failure.

When several indegree-zero vertices are available, any is valid. The current deque order depends on initial vertex numbering and adjacency-list order. For the lexicographically smallest order, replace the queue with a min-heap, giving a loose bound of O((V+E)log V). Do not describe an arbitrary valid order as the unique answer.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: The code retains the full adjacency list and indegree array. Handle parallel edges consistently: decrement exactly as many times as edges were added. Initially isolated vertices must also be enqueued, rather than considering only vertices appearing in edges. The topological order of an empty graph is an empty list. An exception communicates failure more clearly than returning a partial order that callers may mistake for a valid schedule.

time: O(V+E).
space: O(V+E).

walkthrough: 0 and 1 initially have indegree zero.
2 can enter the queue only after both are removed.
Removing 2 releases 3.

pitfalls: Do not return an incomplete order as the answer for a cyclic graph.
Parallel-edge counts and removals must agree.

title: Dijkstra: The Array Version for Dense Graphs
summary: Nonnegative weights make the smallest unsettled distance safe to finalize permanently.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: Find the shortest distance from a source to every vertex in a directed weighted graph, requiring every edge weight to be nonnegative. This version uses an adjacency matrix. math.inf denotes no edge, zero-weight edges remain valid, and only the minimum weight is retained for parallel edges. An inf distance means unreachable, and the source's distance to itself is zero. Any negative-weight input is rejected immediately.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Maintain dist as the best currently known path lengths and fixed as the set of vertices whose distances are final. Each round, linearly scan unsettled vertices for the minimum-distance u, finalize it, and try updating every neighbor through u. Relax only if dist[u]+w is smaller than the current value. Each candidate represents an actual existing path rather than an arbitrary estimate.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Nonnegative weights ensure that subsequent movement among unsettled vertices cannot reduce a path's prefix length. If a shorter route to u existed, its first unsettled vertex after leaving the settled set would have a candidate no greater than that route's length. It could not be settled later than the currently minimum u. This proves the greedy choice; a negative edge breaks the argument.

For an undirected nonnegative graph, the two directions of an input edge share a weight and can both be written during matrix construction. Do not reverse edges temporarily during relaxation: the algorithm must consistently operate on one fixed graph. A single-target query may stop when that target is finalized, but tentative distances to other vertices may then remain incorrect.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: If no finite-distance candidate exists, every remaining vertex is unreachable. Stop immediately rather than adding weights to inf. Matrix initialization, repeated vertex selection, and relaxation all require quadratic work, making this suitable for dense graphs and moderately sized teaching examples. Use true inf in Python, avoiding a fixed large integer that a valid long path could exceed.

time: O(V²+E).
space: O(V²).

walkthrough: Finalize 0 first, then 2.
The route through 2 reduces the tentative distance to 1 from 4 to 3.
Vertex 3 remains unreachable.

pitfalls: Negative edges are invalid even when no negative cycle exists.
Do not use zero to denote a missing edge.

title: Dijkstra: The Priority-Queue Version
summary: A heap selects the smallest candidate distance; stale-entry checks keep relaxation updates simple.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: The quadratic scan of matrix Dijkstra wastes work on sparse directed graphs. An adjacency list stores only actual edges, and a min-heap quickly selects the vertex with the smallest current distance. Weights must be nonnegative. Isolated and unreachable vertices receive inf. For an undirected graph, expand each edge into both directions before calling the same function.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Whenever a distance improves, push a new (distance, vertex) pair without removing the old candidate. If a popped d differs from dist[u], a shorter route has superseded that entry; skip it. For a valid entry, scan u's outgoing edges, maintaining dist as the smallest length among paths discovered so far.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: The min-heap pops valid candidates in the same order as the array version selects the smallest unsettled vertex, so the nonnegative-weight proof still applies. Requiring strict improvement prevents zero-weight cycles from causing endless pushes. No additional fixed set is needed: a valid pop cannot later receive a smaller distance, and stale-entry checks filter repeated processing.

When every weight is one, BFS is simpler than the heap version and runs in linear time. When weights are only zero or one, 0-1 BFS can use a deque. A heap is useful because it orders candidates with differing costs, rather than being automatically a better choice. With many parallel edges, retaining only the lightest edge for each endpoint pair can reduce heap pressure.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: heapq has no direct decrease-key operation. Lazy deletion is simpler, but the heap may reach O(E) size, requiring log(E+1) when parallel edges are allowed. Validate every edge weight, rather than only reachable edges, for a consistent input contract. The template returns only distances; save predecessors during successful relaxation to reconstruct paths.

time: O(V+E log(E+1)) for this heap implementation allowing parallel edges.
space: O(V+E) for the adjacency list and heap, including possible stale entries.

walkthrough: The heap first stores distance 10 for vertex 1.
The route through 2 improves it to 3; the old distance-10 entry is later skipped.

pitfalls: Do not expand stale heap entries again.
Equal candidate distances do not require additional heap entries.

title: Bellman–Ford: Shortest Paths with Negative Edges
summary: Repeatedly relax every edge and detect negative cycles reachable from the source.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: Bellman–Ford solves single-source shortest paths in directed graphs and allows negative edges. If the source can reach a negative cycle, at least some shortest distances have no finite minimum. This implementation raises ValueError rather than returning numbers that continue decreasing after a fixed number of rounds. An unreachable negative cycle does not affect this source and does not cause an error.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Initially only the source has distance zero; every other distance is inf. Each round scans every edge u→v and updates v if u is reachable and dist[u]+w is smaller. Relaxation uses the current array in place, so one round may propagate information across multiple edges. Rounds therefore do not exactly correspond to path edge counts, but each propagates at least one more layer, which is sufficient for correctness.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Without a reachable negative cycle, a shortest route can discard nonnegative cycles to become a simple path of at most V-1 edges. After V-1 rounds, all such paths have been covered. If another check still finds a relaxable edge, reachable routes can continue reducing their costs through a cycle, establishing a negative cycle reachable from the source.

A reachable negative cycle does not make every vertex's shortest distance undefined. Only destinations reachable onward from that cycle are affected. The template raises a single error to give callers a clear failure state, rather than outputting negative infinity vertex by vertex. For finer results, use vertices that can still improve in the detection round as seeds, then search outgoing edges to find all affected vertices.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: Exclude inf starting distances before computing candidates, ensuring that unreachable regions do not participate. If a round makes no updates, stop early because every edge already satisfies the relaxation inequalities. The code retains an explicit negative-cycle check and applies the same condition even after early termination. Callers can use try/except to distinguish finite solutions from undefined cases.

time: O(VE), with fewer rounds possible when convergence occurs early.
space: O(V), without copying the edge list.

walkthrough: 0→1→2 costs 2, better than the direct cost of 5.
The next round makes no improvement, so the result is stable.

pitfalls: In-place rounds do not correspond to exact edge-count layers.
Finite numbers obtained after detecting a negative cycle are not shortest distances.

title: SPFA: Process Only Vertices Whose Distances Change
summary: A queue reduces unproductive scans, but worst-case time remains O(VE), and negative cycles must not cause endless updates.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: SPFA is a work-queue form of Bellman–Ford for single-source problems that may contain negative edges. After a vertex's distance decreases, only its outgoing edges can lead to new improvements, so enqueue that vertex for processing. It is not guaranteed to outperform heap Dijkstra; Dijkstra is generally preferred for nonnegative graphs.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: queue stores vertices whose updated distances have not yet been expanded, while in_queue records whether they are already waiting. After successfully relaxing a neighbor v, enqueue it only if it is not already queued, preventing multiple simultaneous entries for the same vertex. Clear the flag when a vertex is dequeued, because a later improvement must be able to enqueue it again.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: A negative cycle prevents the queue from stabilizing. For each improving candidate route, this version records its edge count as depth[v]=depth[u]+1. If it reaches V, the route must repeat a vertex; the repeated portion arising from strict improvements indicates a reachable negative cycle, so raise an exception. A vertex's ordinary relaxation count is not its route edge count; these quantities have different meanings.

A vertex may improve several times while waiting in the queue. Retain only its latest distance, which will be used when it is expanded. A queue position does not mean its shortest distance is finalized, unlike Dijkstra's settlement order. In particular, do not return when the target is first dequeued: negative edges can allow later branches to improve it again.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: Only strict decreases update distances, so zero-weight cycles do not keep the queue running. Adjacency lists scan only edges of dequeued vertices, which may save practical work. Adversarial graphs can still repeatedly enqueue vertices and reach O(VE). This implementation uses inf for unreachable vertices, raises negative-cycle errors only for the source-reachable portion, and assumes valid endpoint labels.

code:
from collections import deque
from math import inf

def spfa(n, edges, source):
    if not 0 <= source < n:
        raise ValueError("invalid source")
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u,v,w in edges:
        graph[u].append((v,w))
    dist = [inf] * n
    depth = [0] * n
    in_queue = [False] * n
    dist[source] = 0
    queue = deque([source])
    in_queue[source] = True
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        in_queue[u] = False
        for v,w in graph[u]:
            if dist[u]+w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = dist[u]+w
                depth[v] = depth[u]+1
                if depth[v] >= n:
                    raise ValueError("reachable negative cycle")
                if not in_queue[v]:
                    in_queue[v] = True
                    queue.append(v)
    return dist
time: O(VE) in the worst case; there is no general linear-time guarantee.
space: O(V+E) for the adjacency list, queue, and state arrays.

walkthrough: 0 first discovers vertex 1 at cost 5.
Expanding 2 improves vertex 1 to -2, re-enqueueing it if needed.

pitfalls: Clear in_queue when dequeueing.
Stop on a reachable negative cycle rather than allowing endless queue processing.

title: Bellman–Ford: Detect a Negative Cycle Anywhere
summary: Initialize every distance to zero, equivalent to adding a super-source that reaches the whole graph.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: A negative cycle is a directed closed walk with negative total weight; repeatedly traversing it reduces route cost without bound. This lesson tests for a negative cycle anywhere in the graph, rather than only within the region reachable from a particular source. The initializations differ: ordinary single-source Bellman–Ford sets unreachable distances to inf and ignores negative cycles in other components.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Set every initial dist value to zero. This is equivalent to adding a super-source with zero-weight edges to every vertex, making all components reachable. Relax all original edges each round. If a round changes nothing, all edges already satisfy the distance inequalities and further rounds cannot update anything, so return False immediately.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Perform V rounds of relaxation for V original vertices. Without negative cycles, a path after the super-source uses at most V-1 original edges and stabilizes before the final round. A strict improvement in round V indicates a cycle that can keep reducing distances, so return True. A negative self-loop improves in the first round and is correctly detected even when V=1.

A negative edge is not a negative cycle: a single directed edge of weight -5 is entirely valid in an acyclic graph. Conversely, a cycle with mostly positive edges may still have negative total weight, so the combined effect of a cycle matters. Zero initialization does not guess actual shortest distances; it supplies potential values that activate relaxation in every component, which suits an existence test.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: This function returns a Boolean for a graph-wide negative-cycle test, without raising an exception, because finding such a cycle is its normal purpose. A shortest-path interface instead needs an explicit error or special state. Zero-weight and positive-weight cycles are not false positives because updates require strict improvement. An empty graph has no cycles: the loop does not run and the function returns False.

time: O(VE).
space: O(V).

walkthrough: Even if 0 cannot reach 2 or 3, both are initialized as reachable.
The cycle has weight -1 and therefore permits repeated improvements.

pitfalls: Graph-wide detection must cover components unreachable from a chosen source.
The criterion is a strict update in round V, rather than the mere presence of a negative edge.

title: Shortest Paths Using At Most K Edges
summary: Read only the previous round's snapshot to prevent chaining multiple edges within one round.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: Given a directed weighted graph, a source, and a nonnegative integer K, find the minimum cost to every vertex using at most K edges. Negative edges and even negative cycles are allowed: the edge limit bounds route lengths, so the answer remains meaningful. The requirement is at most K edges, rather than exactly K. The source can use zero edges, giving initial cost zero.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Define dist[v] at layer t as the minimum cost to v using at most t edges. To form layer t+1, first copy the old dist to preserve solutions using fewer edges, then consider old[u]+w for every edge u→v. Every transition reads old rather than the new array being written, so each candidate adds exactly one edge.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Any route using at most t+1 edges either already uses at most t, or loses its final edge to leave a prefix using at most t. Copying covers the first case and edge relaxation covers the second, proving the recurrence by induction. In-place relaxation can propagate a long chain within one round according to edge order, violating K and producing invalid answers.

When a problem permits at most K intermediate stops, that usually means at most K+1 flight segments. Read whether endpoints count as stops before converting the budget. Another common mistake is storing only an unrestricted best value per vertex: a cheaper prefix that uses more edges may leave insufficient budget to reach the target. The edge count must therefore be a separate dynamic-programming dimension.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: An unreachable starting vertex cannot produce a transition, so first check whether old[u] is inf. With K=0, return the initial array; reject negative K as invalid input. Stop early if no value changes, because the next layer cannot improve either. No negative-cycle error is needed here: a negative cycle can be used only within the finite budget, unlike unrestricted shortest paths.

time: O(V+K(V+E)); each layer includes an array copy.
space: O(V) for the old and new layer arrays.

walkthrough: In one round, the direct edge to 2 is usable at cost 10.
0→1→2 needs two edges and cannot be chained within this round.

pitfalls: Copy the array: assigning old=dist and then writing into that same list is still wrong.
For exactly K edges, do not preserve the old layer; initialize each new layer to inf.

title: Floyd–Warshall: All-Pairs Shortest Paths
summary: Expand the set of permitted intermediate vertices layer by layer; the intermediate vertex must be the outermost loop.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: Find shortest distances between every pair of vertices in a directed weighted graph. Initialize dist[i][j] to the minimum direct-edge weight, dist[i][i]=0, and other entries to inf. Negative edges are allowed, but this function raises ValueError upon detecting any negative cycle because some pairwise shortest distances then lack a finite definition.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Dynamic-programming layer k permits only vertices numbered at most k as intermediate vertices. A shortest route either avoids k and keeps the old value, or passes through k and splits into i→k and k→j, whose distances sum to a candidate. Thus the update is dist[i][j]=min(dist[i][j],dist[i][k]+dist[k][j]).

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Putting k in the outermost loop ensures that each round really expands the permitted intermediate-vertex set by one. Without negative cycles, a shortest route can be a simple path, so splitting does not require repeated uses of k; in-place updates are valid. After every k has been processed, all vertices may serve as intermediates, yielding all-pairs shortest distances.

To reconstruct routes, maintain next[i][j] as the next stop when traveling from i to j. A successful improvement through k copies next[i][k]. Retain a separate marker when no path exists. If only reachability is required, replace the minimum-plus update with Boolean AND and OR to obtain transitive closure. Boolean closure and weighted distances are different quantities.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: Skip candidates with an inf segment to avoid adding unreachable routes. In particular, adding a negative edge to a fixed large integer must not fabricate reachability. Keep the minimum of parallel edges, and do not overwrite a negative self-loop with diagonal zero. At the end, any dist[v][v]<0 reveals a negative cycle. A more detailed pairwise interface could mark affected pairs individually, but this version raises a single error.

time: O(V³+E).
space: O(V²), including the output matrix.

example.output: The shortest distance from 0 to 2 is 1
walkthrough: The direct distance 0→2 is initialized to 5.
Allowing 1 as an intermediate gives candidate 2+(-1)=1, replacing the previous value.

pitfalls: The intermediate vertex k must be the outermost loop.
Retain negative self-loops so negative cycles can be detected.

title: A*: Minimum Knight Moves on a Finite Board
summary: Guide knight-route search with a provable lower-bound heuristic while preserving BFS shortest-path correctness.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: The board is a finite rows×cols rectangle with zero-based coordinates. A knight moves by (±1,±2) or (±2,±1), at unit cost per move. A blocked collection may specify forbidden cells, and both endpoints must lie on the board. Return the minimum move count, or -1 if unreachable. A blocked endpoint also returns -1. This is not a distance formula for an infinite board.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Let dx and dy be the absolute coordinate differences to the goal. One move reduces Manhattan distance by at most three and either coordinate difference by at most two. Therefore h=max(ceil((dx+dy)/3),ceil(max(dx,dy)/2)) is a necessary lower bound on the number of moves. Obstacles can only increase the real distance and do not invalidate this bound. Ordinary Manhattan distance itself is not a valid estimate of knight moves.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: A* orders states by f=g+h, where g is the actual number of moves from the start. Each of the two lower bounds decreases by at most one along a legal edge, and their maximum still satisfies h(u)≤1+h(v), the consistency condition. Consequently, when the goal is popped as a valid heap entry, its g is shortest. Stopping when the goal is first discovered is invalid: another branch may still produce a shorter route.

The closer a heuristic is to the actual distance, the more effectively it usually avoids irrelevant directions, but stronger estimates still require proof. Finite-board boundaries can force detours, and small boards can split into disconnected regions, so the coordinate lower bound is not an answer formula. Setting h to zero reduces the algorithm to unit-weight Dijkstra and provides a correctness comparison.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: The code retains the best known g for each state, pushes only strict improvements, and skips stale heap entries. Coordinates in heap entries allow stable comparisons without affecting correctness. Heuristics often reduce exploration, but the worst case may still visit the entire board. Check the finite boundaries: without them, an unreachable instance may explore an infinite state space and never terminate.

time: O(RC log(RC+1)); each cell of the finite board has at most eight edges.
space: O(RC+B), where B is the number of distinct coordinates in blocked, including the heap and best distances.

walkthrough: The goal is one legal knight move away.
The starting heuristic is one; when the goal is popped, g=1.

pitfalls: Ordinary Manhattan distance can overestimate the required number of knight moves.
Do not return when the goal first enters the heap.
Do not confuse finite-board restrictions with an infinite-board problem.

title: Shortest-Path Algorithm Summary
summary: Identify weight conditions, query scope, and edge limits before choosing a shortest-path model.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: The first question in a shortest-path problem is what cost means. When every edge has equal cost, BFS levels give the minimum edge count directly. With nonnegative weights, Dijkstra greedily finalizes the smallest candidate. With negative edges, Bellman–Ford avoids that greedy assumption but must handle negative cycles. Algorithm names cannot replace input conditions: using Dijkstra despite negative edges is a modeling error.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Query scope also determines the tool. A single BFS or Dijkstra run suits a small number of queries from one source. Many arbitrary-pair queries on a small graph can use Floyd's quadratic storage and cubic preprocessing. SPFA uses a queue to reduce unproductive edge scans but has no better worst-case guarantee than Bellman–Ford. A* uses a proven distance lower bound to guide expansion toward one target.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: An edge budget changes the state: at most K edges requires layered transitions from the previous round's snapshot, not chained in-place relaxation. A negative cycle makes unrestricted route costs unbounded below, but affects only finitely many candidates under a finite K-edge budget. The inf marker for unreachable vertices differs from an undefined distance due to a negative cycle. Interfaces should express these through different mechanisms rather than treating both as ordinary numbers.

After choosing an algorithm, check the output semantics: does the distance include the starting state, is an actual path needed, and may vertices be revisited? Word Ladder returns a word count, while the knight problem returns a move count. Both use unit-edge searches but follow different counting conventions. Examples, tests, and interface documentation must cover these distinctions together to prevent off-by-one answers despite correct algorithms.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: The checking function below tests whether finite distance labels satisfy the source condition and all edge-relaxation inequalities. It is a debugging aid, not a standalone proof of optimality: arbitrarily low labels may satisfy the inequalities as well. Each finite label must also be known to come from a real path. Path feasibility together with the absence of any improving edge supports correctness.

time: O(V+E) is a loose upper bound; after checking the list length, this implementation scans edges in O(E).
space: O(1), without copying the input.

walkthrough: The source has distance zero.
For both edges, the destination distance is at most the starting distance plus edge weight.
Actual paths achieve these labels; only together with the inequalities does this establish optimality.

pitfalls: Constraint checking is not a complete shortest-path algorithm.
Unreachability and negative-cycle reports have different meanings.

title: Graph Theory Summary: Choose Tools by States and Invariants
summary: Connectivity, dependencies, minimum connection cost, and shortest routes are four distinct objectives.

sections.heading: Problem and modeling
paragraphs: The first step in graph modeling is to express the problem using vertices and edges. Grid cells, words, and board positions can all be implicit-graph states, with neighbor-generation rules defining permitted moves. Direction determines whether reachability is symmetric, and weights determine whether levels equal cost. Clarifying these conditions is necessary to explain precisely what a visited set or distance array represents.

sections.heading: Core invariant
paragraphs: Both DFS and BFS traverse connected regions. Island counts, areas, and boundary escape require complete component coverage, while BFS additionally suits unit-edge shortest paths. Backtracking to enumerate paths preserves branch history: a global visited set must not erase distinct prefixes. Reverse search suits states flowing toward common destinations, as in reversing ocean-flow edges.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Union-find represents undirected components that continually merge and suits path-existence queries, redundant edges, and Kruskal. Prim and Kruskal minimize the total cost of connecting the graph; Dijkstra minimizes route costs from a source. These are not interchangeable objectives. Topological sorting represents precedence dependencies and detects cycles through unprocessed vertices. It requires a directed graph and does not apply to ordinary undirected connectivity.

Finally, test invariants with extreme graphs: an empty graph, a single vertex, a long chain, a pure cycle, multiple components, parallel edges, and self-loops expose different problems. For grids, also check a single row, a single column, all water, and all land. Tests do more than check a number: they verify model promises, including whether input is preserved, failures are explicit, and unreachable markers are consistent.

sections.heading: Python implementation details
paragraphs: Make failure states explicit: use a sentinel for unreachability and report an error when a spanning tree does not exist or a negative cycle makes shortest distances undefined. The function below returns connected components of an undirected graph and can serve as a starting point for analyzing other models. An explicit stack avoids deep recursion, isolated vertices become singleton components, and an empty graph returns an empty list. Component order follows vertex-number scanning.

time: O(V+E).
space: O(V+E), including the adjacency list and output.

walkthrough: Each of the two edges forms a two-vertex component.
Vertex 4 does not appear in the edge list but still forms its own component.

pitfalls: Undirected components do not substitute for directed strongly connected components.
Include visited records, the stack, and result storage in space complexity.
